summary.text: A paleographic account interprets damaged Shang forms as a bear-like 能, but another disputes that reading and places securely identified examples in Western Zhou bronze. The character is also attested for “be able” and “ability”; the evidence does not establish how these uses relate to the bear sense.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph is interpreted as depicting a bear. This construction is qualified because the proposed Shang examples are disputed; the earliest securely identified graph is placed in Western Zhou bronze by one account. The Han dictionary instead segments the graph as 肉 plus 㠯 and calls 㠯 phonetic, but paleographic discussion allows that shape to reflect the bear’s altered head, so no separate phonetic component is established.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a bear-like animal, with head, body, limbs, and short tail. Its identification in damaged Shang forms is disputed; this is a whole-picture analysis, not a split into modern shapes.

history.text: Some damaged Shang oracle-bone forms have been identified as 能 and described as bear-like, but their use is unclear. A competing analysis rejects that identification and places securely identifiable examples in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions. Descriptions of the graphic sequence report the head changing toward 㠯, the body rendered as 月 (肉), and the feet arranged side by side; these descriptions do not settle the disputed Shang reading.

The Han dictionary records 能 as a kind of bear and analyzes it as 肉 plus 㠯. Its account links the animal’s firmness and strength with 賢能 and 能傑; this documents the dictionary’s interpretation, not a demonstrated historical path from bear to ability.

uncertainties.text: The Shang identification and use remain disputed, and no dated first occurrence is established for the Western Zhou examples. The bear’s spoken name is not independently known here, and the evidence does not show whether the ability word developed from the bear word or whether the graph was reused for it because of sound.

The Han dictionary’s analysis of 㠯 as phonetic is historically important, but paleographic discussion also allows it to reflect the transformed bear head. No independent phonetic role or component sound comparison is established.

senses.text: The Han dictionary defines 能 as a kind of bear, and historical pronunciation records distinguish bear readings. Proposed Shang examples do not securely date this use because their identification and use are disputed.
A reported Western Zhou bronze use has 能 as a verb meaning “be able to.” This is the earliest ability use identified here; it does not establish the character’s original meaning.
Historical reports cite ability-related noun uses in Warring States-era texts. Modern definitions include “ability,” but do not establish a further dated stage.

limitations.text: The bear and ability uses are separately attested, but their semantic relationship or a sound-based borrowing between them is not established. The evidence gives no independently known spoken name for the depicted bear to demonstrate a sound match.

The bear-like Shang forms are disputed: some scholars identify them as 能, while others read them as a different graph, and their use is unclear. The cited materials discuss Western Zhou bronze forms but provide no verified glyph image to show.
